```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.2, dpi = 150,
                      out.width = "100%")
# the alt text of the charts, for screen readers: the curve, the scales under it and what is
# particular to each chart
alt <- function(scales, more = "") {
  paste0("The standard normal curve, divided at every standard deviation and marked with the ",
         "percentage of cases in each interval, above the ", scales, " scales", more, ".")
}
standard <- "z, T, cumulative percentage, percentile, sten, stanine, grade and IQ"
```

`plot_normal()` draws the standard normal curve with score scales lined up under it, so that a
score on one scale can be read off on the others. This article starts from the default chart and
works up to charts with scales of your own.

```{r setup}
library(snp)
```

## The default chart

```{r default, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", in blues")}
plot_normal()
```

The curve is divided at every standard deviation and marked with the percentage of cases in each
interval. Under it are the z, T, cumulative percentage, percentile, sten, stanine, grade and IQ
scales. Read straight down from any point: a score one standard deviation above the mean is z = 1,
T = 60 and IQ = 115, 84.1% of cases fall below it, and it is in stanine 7 and grade B.

## Palettes

`palette` sets the colours. In `"blues"` (the default), `"reds"` and `"greens"`, colour shows how
common a score is: the intervals under the curve that hold more cases are darker, and so are the
bands nearer the mean.

```{r reds, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", in reds")}
plot_normal(palette = "reds")
```

```{r greens, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", in greens")}
plot_normal(palette = "greens")
```

`"diverging"` leaves the area under the curve gray and colours the bands by where they sit against
the mean: blue below it, red above it, darker the further from it, and gray for a band centred on
it.

```{r diverging, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", the area under the curve gray and the bands blue below the mean and red above it")}
plot_normal(palette = "diverging")
```

## Dark mode

`mode = "dark"` draws light text on a near-black background, for slides and dark pages. The
colours that are darker in the light mode are brighter instead, so that they still stand out from
the background.

```{r dark, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", in blues on a near-black background")}
plot_normal(mode = "dark")
```

```{r dark-greens, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", in greens on a near-black background")}
plot_normal(palette = "greens", mode = "dark")
```

```{r dark-diverging, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", with blue and red bands on a near-black background")}
plot_normal(palette = "diverging", mode = "dark")
```

## Text size

The chart keeps its proportions, about 2.2 times as wide as it is tall, so text that is the right
size on a small figure is too small on a large one. `size` is the text size in millimetres: the
default of 3 suits figures about 7 inches wide, and about 5 suits figures about 12 inches wide.
The lines, the gaps between the bands and their rounded corners grow with it.

```{r size, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 5.6, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", in blues, with text sized for a figure 12 inches wide")}
plot_normal(size = 5)
```

## Saving

`plot_normal()` returns a ggplot object, so `ggsave()` saves it. A figure with the proportions of
the chart has no empty margins:

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
ggsave("normal.png", plot_normal(), width = 7, height = 3.2)
```

For print, papers and slides, save it as vector graphics instead, which stay sharp at any size: PDF,
SVG, EMF or EPS, all in [Saving as vector graphics](vector-graphics.html).

## The scales as data

The scales under the curve are a data frame, which `standard_normal_scales_data()` returns:

```{r data}
scales <- standard_normal_scales_data()
head(scales)
unique(scales$scale)
```

Each row is a tick mark or a band:

- `scale`: the name of the scale, shown at the left of its row. Rows are drawn from top to bottom
  in the order the names first appear.
- `z`: where the tick mark goes on the z axis, or where the band starts.
- `z_end`: where the band ends, or `NA` for a tick mark.
- `label`: the text at the tick mark or inside the band.
- `colour`: the fill of the band, or `NA` for the colours of the palette.

Change the data frame and pass it to `plot_normal()` as its first argument, `scales`. Every scale
you add makes the chart taller, so the figures below change height with the number of scales.

## Choosing scales

Keep the rows of the scales you want:

```{r keep, fig.height = 2.7, fig.alt = alt("z, T and IQ")}
plot_normal(scales[scales$scale %in% c("z", "T", "IQ"), ])
```

Sort the rows to change the order of the scales:

```{r reorder, fig.height = 2.6, fig.alt = alt("IQ, percentile, stanine and z")}
wanted <- c("IQ", "PERCENTILE", "STANINE", "z")
reordered <- scales[scales$scale %in% wanted, ]
reordered <- reordered[order(match(reordered$scale, wanted)), ]
plot_normal(reordered)
```

Rename a scale by changing its `scale` column:

```{r rename, fig.height = 3.3, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", the z scale renamed Z SCORE and the cumulative percentage scale renamed % BELOW")}
renamed <- scales
renamed$scale[renamed$scale == "z"] <- "Z SCORE"
renamed$scale[renamed$scale == "CUMULATIVE %"] <- "% BELOW"
plot_normal(renamed)
```

## Adding tick marks

Any scale that is a linear transformation of z, a mean plus a number of standard deviations, is a
row of tick marks. A small function makes them, in the columns of the standard scales so that
`rbind()` can join them:

```{r linear-scale}
linear_scale <- function(name, mean, sd, z = -3:3) {
  data.frame(scale = name, z = z, z_end = NA, label = mean + sd * z, colour = NA)
}
```

Wechsler subtest scaled scores have a mean of 10 and a standard deviation of 3, and CEEB scores a
mean of 500 and a standard deviation of 100:

```{r add, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = alt("z, T, cumulative percentage, percentile, sten, stanine, grade, IQ, Wechsler scaled score and CEEB")}
plot_normal(rbind(scales, linear_scale("SCALED", 10, 3), linear_scale("CEEB", 500, 100)))
```

Tick marks need not sit at whole standard deviations. Normal curve equivalents (NCE) have a mean
of 50 and a standard deviation of 21.06, and are usually labelled at round values, each placed at
its own z. NCE 1, 50 and 99 fall on the 1st, 50th and 99th percentiles:

```{r nce, fig.height = 2.4, fig.alt = alt("z, percentile and normal curve equivalent", ", where NCE 1, 50 and 99 line up with the 1st, 50th and 99th percentiles")}
nce <- c(1, 10, 25, 50, 75, 90, 99)
nce_scale <- data.frame(scale = "NCE", z = (nce - 50) / 21.06, z_end = NA, label = nce, colour = NA)
plot_normal(rbind(scales[scales$scale %in% c("z", "PERCENTILE"), ], nce_scale))
```

## Adding bands

A band runs from `z` to `z_end`. `qnorm()` gives the z at which a percentage of cases falls
below, so it cuts bands that hold equal shares of cases, such as quartiles and deciles:

```{r quantiles, fig.height = 2.4, fig.alt = alt("percentile, quartile and decile", ", whose bands each hold an equal share of cases and so narrow towards the mean")}
quantile_bands <- function(name, n) {
  cuts <- qnorm(seq_len(n - 1) / n)
  data.frame(scale = name, z = c(-4, cuts), z_end = c(cuts, 4), label = seq_len(n), colour = NA)
}
plot_normal(rbind(scales[scales$scale == "PERCENTILE", ],
                  quantile_bands("QUARTILE", 4),
                  quantile_bands("DECILE", 10)))
```

Bands in the units of another scale are placed by converting their limits to z, here IQ ranges
one standard deviation wide:

```{r iq-ranges, fig.height = 2.4, fig.alt = alt("percentile, IQ and IQ range", ", the IQ ranges below 70, 70 to 84, 85 to 114, 115 to 129, and 130 and above")}
iq <- c(40, 70, 85, 115, 130, 160)
iq_ranges <- data.frame(scale = "IQ RANGE", z = (head(iq, -1) - 100) / 15, z_end = (iq[-1] - 100) / 15,
                        label = c("<70", "70-84", "85-114", "115-129", "130+"), colour = NA)
plot_normal(rbind(scales[scales$scale %in% c("PERCENTILE", "IQ"), ], iq_ranges))
```

Bands need not cover the whole axis; a row can hold only the bands it needs:

```{r gaps, fig.height = 2.4, fig.alt = alt("z, percentile and extremes", ", the extremes row holding only a Very low band below z = -2 and a Very high band above z = 2")}
extremes <- data.frame(scale = "EXTREMES", z = c(-4, 2), z_end = c(-2, 4),
                       label = c("Very low", "Very high"), colour = NA)
plot_normal(rbind(scales[scales$scale %in% c("z", "PERCENTILE"), ], extremes))
```

## Colouring bands yourself

A band with a `colour` keeps it whatever the palette; the labels on it turn white or near-black,
whichever stands out more. A pass mark one standard deviation below the mean:

```{r decision, fig.height = 2.4, fig.alt = alt("z, T and decision", ", the decision row a red Fail band below z = -1 and a green Pass band above it")}
decision <- data.frame(scale = "DECISION", z = c(-4, -1), z_end = c(-1, 4),
                       label = c("Fail", "Pass"), colour = c("#c74845", "#31902c"))
plot_normal(rbind(scales[scales$scale %in% c("z", "T"), ], decision))
```

Bands with and without a colour can share a row, here stanines 7 to 9 picked out and the rest left
to the palette:

```{r highlight, fig.height = 2.3, fig.alt = alt("z and stanine", ", with stanines 7 to 9 in red")}
stanine <- scales[scales$scale == "STANINE", ]
stanine$colour[stanine$label %in% 7:9] <- "#c74845"
plot_normal(rbind(scales[scales$scale == "z", ], stanine))
```

## Scales of your own only

The scales need not include any of the standard ones. A test with raw scores of mean 24 and
standard deviation 5, and four performance levels cut at raw scores of 15, 22 and 30; the `colour`
column is optional and left out:

```{r own, fig.height = 2.2, fig.alt = alt("raw score and level", ", raw scores from 10 to 40 and the levels Below basic, Basic, Proficient and Advanced, blue below the mean and red above it")}
raw <- seq(10, 40, 5)
cuts <- (c(15, 22, 30) - 24) / 5
test <- rbind(data.frame(scale = "RAW SCORE", z = (raw - 24) / 5, z_end = NA, label = raw),
              data.frame(scale = "LEVEL", z = c(-4, cuts), z_end = c(cuts, 4),
                         label = c("Below basic", "Basic", "Proficient", "Advanced")))
plot_normal(test, palette = "diverging")
```

## Adding to the chart

The chart is a ggplot object, so ggplot2 layers can be added to it. Its x axis is the z axis, and
the curve is `dnorm(z)` high, so a score is easy to place. Mark a score of z = 1.3:

```{r mark, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", with a red point on the curve at z = 1.3")}
score <- 1.3
plot_normal() +
  annotate("point", x = score, y = dnorm(score), size = 3, colour = "#c74845") +
  annotate("text", x = score, y = dnorm(score), label = "z = 1.3", hjust = -0.25, vjust = -0.5,
           size = 3, colour = "#c74845")
```

Shade the 5% of cases furthest from the mean, below z = -1.96 and above z = 1.96:

```{r tails, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", with the 5% of cases below z = -1.96 and above z = 1.96 shaded red")}
upper <- seq(qnorm(0.975), 4, 0.01)
plot_normal(palette = "diverging") +
  annotate("ribbon", x = -upper, ymin = 0, ymax = dnorm(upper), fill = "#c74845", alpha = 0.7) +
  annotate("ribbon", x = upper, ymin = 0, ymax = dnorm(upper), fill = "#c74845", alpha = 0.7)
```

Add a title:

```{r title, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = alt(standard, ", under the title Scores on the standard normal curve")}
plot_normal() + labs(title = "Scores on the standard normal curve")
```
